The male cones are much smaller. They are produced in clusters near the tip of the long shoots. Each male cone is oval in shape and ranges from 1.5 cm to 2.5 cm in length. It consists of spirally arranged specialized leaves known as microsporophylls or stamens around the central cone axis. Each microsporophyll bears two sacs like microsporangia (pollen sac) on the ventral side. The microsporangia produce a large number of microspores (pollen grains). Each microspore or pollen grain is a rounded and yellow-coloured, light, uninucleate structure with two outer covering an inner intine and an outer exine. It has ballon like wings. The wings help in the dispersal of spores by wind.

Female cone The female cones develop laterally in the axil of scale leaves. They are formed in clusters in place of long shoots. They are produced on the lower branches from those of the male cones. There may be one to four cones on each long shoot. Each cone consists of central axis bearing spirally arranged scales. The scales are of two types; bract scales and ovuliferous scales. The bract scales are thin membranous and are directly attached to the central axis. The ovuliferous scales are present on the ventral surface of each bract scale. Each ovuliferous scale bears two ovules (megasporangia), situated side by side on upper side. The ovule (megasporangium) is inverted (i.e. anatropous) has a mass of nucellar tissue surrounded by a single integument. The micropylar end of the ovule is directed towards the central axis. The diploid megaspore mother cell present in the nucellus of ovule undergoes meiosis and forms a linear tetrad of four megaspores. Upper three megaspores degenerate but the lowermost megaspore becomes functional. The functional megaspore (embryo sac) increases in size and occupies the major part of the nucellus. This functional megasprore develop into female gametophyte.

Figure 2.7.2 (a) Female cone (b) L.S. of female cone Pollination and Fertilization Microspore is the first cell of male gametophyte. It germinates inside microsporangium. It divides and forms 4-celled stage (2-prothalial cell, 1-antheridial cell and 1-tube cell). These 4celled stage pollen grains released and pollination takes place. The pollination in Pinus is anemophilous (i.e. takes place by wind). At the time of pollination the ovule secrete mucilaginous fluid from the micropyle and pollen grains entangled on it. These pollen grains, then, draws into the pollen chamber and remain inactive for few months. Then, tube cell project to form pollen tube, which elongate towards the archegonium. The antheridial cell divides to form stalk cell and body cell. The body cell again divides to form two motile unequal male nuclei.

The functional megaspore is the first cell of the female gametophyte. Two to four cells of the female gametophyte at the micropylar end function as archegonial initials and form two to four flask shaped archegonia. Each archegonium consists of a large venter, a short neck and a very large egg or oosphere. The neck is without neck canal cells.

The fertilization takes place after about one year of pollination. The pollen tube containing two male nuclei elongates and penetrates the archegonium through micropyle and reaches up to the egg. One of the male nuclei fuses with the egg forming diploid zygote (oospore) and the remaining one get degenerated. The zygote is the first cell of sporophyte. The fertilized egg (Zygote) undergoes mitotic division and develops into embryo. After fertilization, integument and megasporangium are converted into seed coat and seed respectively. A mature embryo consists of radicle towards the micropylar end and plumule towards the inner side. It is surrounded by cotyledons. Some part of the ovuliferous scale fuses with the developing seed to form wing, which helps in dispersal in air. Seeds are generally dispersed by wind. Under favourable conditions, the seed germinates into new sporophyte.
Figure 2.7.3 Life cycle of Pinus 2.7.4 ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF GYMNOSPERM Gymnosperms are economically most important plants. The economic importances of gymnosperm are explained below:
1. Ornamental importance: Species of Cycas are used for decoration purposes. Many gymnosperms are cultivated in the gardens as ornamental plants.

2. Source of food : The cycads are used as food in many parts of the world. They are eaten as a source of starch which is obtained from stem or seed of cycads. Seeds of Pinus gerardiana (chilgoza) are edible.

3. Source of wood: Many gymnosperm trees are of great importance for their light colour, straight grained and light weighed soft wood. The wood is used as timber as building materials, furniture, packing case, match box, pencils, railways sleepers, fuels, etc.

4. Medicinal importance: Species of Ephedra yield ephedrine (alkaloid) which is used in treatment of asthma, cough, cold, bronchitis, etc. Anti-cancerous drug (taxol) is obtained from the bark of Taxus.
